02-Knowledge/Databases/Vector_Search/Vec.title: Vector Search Technologies — Selection Guide
02-Knowledge/Databases/Vector_Search/Vec.content:
Draft 
                  
                

Work in progress — may be incomplete or change.


Choosing a Vector Search Technology
Vector search retrieves items by similarity between their numerical representations (embeddings). It is commonly used for semantic search, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), recommendations, and similarity-based discovery.
The right technology depends on the workload, existing infrastructure, filtering requirements, scale, and operational constraints. There is no universally best vector database.
1. Understand the technology categories
These tools solve related problems, but they are not interchangeable.






























CategoryTechnologiesWhat you getDedicated vector databasesMilvus, Qdrant, Weaviate, ChromaVector storage, indexing, retrieval APIs, and varying levels of filtering and distributed operationsRelational database extensionpgvectorVector search integrated with PostgreSQL tables, SQL, transactions, and existing database operationsSimilarity-search libraryFAISSLow-level indexing and nearest-neighbor search algorithms embedded in your applicationSearch enginesOpenSearch, ElasticsearchKeyword search, filtering, aggregations, and vector search within a broader search platform
Important: A vector index, a vector database, and a complete retrieval system are different layers. A library such as FAISS can provide the search engine, but your application must supply the surrounding storage, API, metadata, security, and operational capabilities.
2. Technology comparison
Dedicated vector databases


Milvus

Designed for large-scale vector retrieval and distributed deployments.
Offers Lite, Standalone, and Distributed deployment modes.
Consider when workload scale, throughput, and independent resource scaling justify additional infrastructure.
Trade-off: distributed deployments introduce operational complexity.
Detailed note: Milvus.



Qdrant

Dedicated vector database with strong payload filtering.
Supports dense, sparse, and multi-vector search, along with hybrid retrieval.
Consider when filtering, retrieval quality, and production-oriented vector operations are important.
Trade-off: still requires operating and tuning a dedicated service unless using managed infrastructure.



Weaviate

Dedicated vector database with integrated keyword and vector hybrid search.
Offers self-managed and managed deployment options.
Consider when hybrid retrieval and its data model and integration ecosystem fit the application.
Trade-off: evaluate its schema, query model, and operational footprint against simpler alternatives.



Chroma

Developer-friendly option for embedding and retrieval workflows.
Supports in-memory, persistent local, and remote-server client patterns.
Consider for experimentation, local applications, and straightforward retrieval prototypes.
Trade-off: evaluate deployment, availability, and operational requirements before choosing it for a production service.



Other vector-search approaches


pgvector

Adds vector similarity search to PostgreSQL.
Supports exact search and approximate indexes such as HNSW and IVFFlat.
Consider when relational data, SQL queries, transactions, and vector retrieval belong together.
Trade-off: performance depends on data volume, indexing, filtering patterns, and PostgreSQL capacity. It is not inherently unsuitable for large workloads; benchmark the actual workload before ruling it out.



FAISS

A library for efficient similarity search and clustering.
Offers multiple index families and CPU/GPU implementations.
Supports index serialization and loading.
Consider when you need low-level control over retrieval algorithms and can build the surrounding application infrastructure.
Trade-off: it does not provide a complete database service, multi-tenant API, or operational control plane.
Detailed note: FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search).



OpenSearch / Elasticsearch

Search platforms that combine keyword and vector retrieval.
Useful when full-text search, filters, aggregations, and hybrid ranking are important parts of the same workload.
Consider when an existing search platform can serve both lexical and semantic retrieval.
Trade-off: vector workloads must be evaluated alongside the search cluster’s indexing, storage, and operational requirements.



3. Choose based on workload





































RequirementTechnologies worth evaluatingLocal experimentation and quick prototypesChroma, Milvus LiteExisting PostgreSQL applicationpgvectorDedicated vector retrieval serviceQdrant, WeaviateLarge-scale distributed vector workloadsMilvusLow-level algorithmic control or custom retrieval serviceFAISSKeyword + semantic search in one platformOpenSearch, ElasticsearchExisting search infrastructureEvaluate its native vector capabilities first
These are starting points, not universal rankings. A technology that fits a small prototype may not fit a high-availability production system.
4. Evaluation criteria
Before selecting a technology, evaluate:

Data characteristics: vector count, dimensions, embedding model, metadata size, update frequency, and growth.
Retrieval quality: exact versus approximate search, recall@k, filtering behavior, and reranking requirements.
Performance: p95/p99 latency, throughput, concurrency, index-build time, and ingestion rate.
Storage and memory: RAM requirements, disk usage, compression, quantization, and replication overhead.
Query capabilities: metadata filtering, keyword search, hybrid retrieval, and multi-vector support.
Reliability: persistence, backup and restore, replication, recovery, and availability.
Security: authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, network boundaries, and data residency.
Operations: deployment complexity, monitoring, upgrades, scaling, and maintenance.
Cost: compute, storage, managed-service pricing, and engineering effort.

Benchmark with representative embeddings, queries, filters, and data distributions. A vector-count estimate alone is not enough to establish capacity.
5. Practical selection principles

Prefer pgvector when PostgreSQL already meets the application’s relational and retrieval requirements.
Prefer a dedicated vector database when vector retrieval needs independent scaling, specialized filtering, or dedicated operational capabilities.
Prefer FAISS when you need a retrieval library and are prepared to own the surrounding system.
Prefer a search engine when keyword search and vector retrieval need to work together.
Avoid choosing based on a vendor’s maximum-vector-count claim or a generic benchmark.
Measure retrieval quality as well as latency; a fast search that misses relevant results is not a successful system.

03-Architecture/ADRs/Data_Engineering/Pa.content:
Draft 
                  
                

Work in progress — may be incomplete or change.


Parquet Bloom Filters for Row-Group Pruning
Decision: Use Parquet Bloom Filters as an additional data-skipping mechanism for selective equality predicates on suitable high-cardinality columns.
Status: Accepted — retain the original decision status; validate the implementation and performance assumptions against actual workloads.
Context
Analytical data lakes commonly store large datasets in Parquet files containing multiple row groups. Queries that filter on selective equality predicates may still read substantial data when existing pruning mechanisms cannot rule out the relevant row groups.
For example:

A query filters on customer_id = 12345.
A row group’s minimum and maximum customer IDs span a wide range.
The queried value falls within that range.
Min/max statistics cannot establish whether the value actually occurs in that row group.

This can cause unnecessary column-chunk reads even when the requested value is absent.
We need a compact membership structure that can establish absence without requiring a full scan of the relevant data.
Decision
Use Bloom Filters as an additional pruning layer for selected Parquet columns.
A Bloom Filter provides a one-sided guarantee:

If it reports that a value is absent, the value is definitely absent.
If it reports that a value may be present, the value must still be checked against the actual data.
False positives are possible; false negatives are not.

This makes Bloom Filters suitable for data skipping because an incorrect positive only causes extra reading. An incorrect negative would risk missing valid records, which the structure prevents.
Proposed pruning model
The following is a conceptual data-skipping flow:

Partition pruning
File-level pruning
Row-group pruning using available statistics
Bloom Filter checks for supported predicates and columns
Read the relevant column chunks and evaluate the query

The actual order and combination of these checks depend on the query engine, file format implementation, and available metadata.
Bloom Filters complement min/max statistics:

Min/max statistics are effective when predicate values fall outside a row group’s value range.
Bloom Filters can rule out equality values that fall inside the range but are not actually present.
Neither mechanism replaces predicate evaluation against the underlying data.

Configuration considerations
A 1% target false-positive probability is a reasonable starting point for evaluation, not a universal requirement.
For a conventional Bloom Filter:

Approximately 9.6 bits per inserted element are required for a 1% false-positive probability.
Approximately 14.4 bits per inserted element are required for a 0.1% false-positive probability.
The optimal number of hash functions depends on the filter size and expected element count.

The actual filter size and effectiveness depend on implementation details, encoding, cardinality, and the number of distinct values inserted.
Column selection
Prioritize columns that satisfy most of these conditions:

Frequently used in selective equality predicates.
Have sufficiently many distinct values for the filter to provide useful discrimination.
Occur in enough queried row groups for the saved I/O to justify filter storage and write overhead.
Have broad or overlapping min/max ranges that limit existing pruning.
Are supported by the writer and reader versions used in the data platform.

Do not enable Bloom Filters indiscriminately on every column. Evaluate their benefit against query frequency, row-group size, data distribution, and filter metadata overhead.
Expected benefits

Reduce unnecessary column-chunk reads for selective equality predicates.
Complement min/max statistics where value ranges are not selective.
Provide bounded-memory membership checks compared with storing exact sets.
Preserve query correctness because false positives cause additional reads rather than missed records.

The actual pruning ratio and query improvement must be measured. They depend on the data distribution, query selectivity, row-group layout, engine support, and cache state.
Costs and limitations

Write overhead: the writer must construct and persist the filters.
Storage overhead: filter data and associated metadata increase file size.
Read overhead: readers must load and evaluate filter metadata.
False positives: some row groups that do not contain the value may still be read.
Immutability: changing the contents of an existing Parquet column chunk requires rewriting the affected data and its metadata.
Compatibility: readers that do not support the relevant Parquet Bloom Filter features may ignore the filters and continue reading data without the expected pruning benefit.

Bloom Filters are not a replacement for partitioning, sorting, clustering, dictionary encoding, or min/max statistics. They are one additional optimization in a broader data-skipping strategy.
Alternatives considered



































AlternativeStrengthLimitation for this use caseHash setExact membership answersUsually much higher memory consumptionBitmap indexEfficient for suitable low- or medium-cardinality domainsCan become expensive for high-cardinality dataMin/max statisticsCompact and effective for rangesCannot reliably distinguish values inside broad rangesCount-Min SketchApproximate frequency estimationAnswers frequency questions, not exact membershipNo additional filterNo filter construction or storage overheadLeaves avoidable reads when existing statistics are ineffective
Validation and rollout
Before enabling filters broadly:

Identify representative equality-filter workloads.
Measure baseline bytes read, row groups scanned, query latency, and write cost.
Enable filters on a small set of suitable columns.
Verify that the writer actually persists the filters.
Confirm that the target query engine recognizes and consults them.
Compare row groups pruned, bytes read, query latency, file size, and write overhead.
Expand only where the overall workload benefits.

Use query plans, scan metrics, Parquet metadata inspection, and engine-specific diagnostics. Do not infer successful pruning merely because a file contains Bloom Filter metadata.
Success criteria

Filters are present for the intended columns and supported by the deployed readers.
Selective equality queries demonstrate measurable reductions in unnecessary reads.
Query performance improves for the targeted workload.
Write latency and storage overhead remain acceptable.
Query results remain identical with filters enabled and disabled.

Numerical targets such as a 1% false-positive probability or a particular row-group skip ratio should be treated as workload-specific acceptance criteria and confirmed through benchmarking.
